Do I not understand it, is there more to it or it is something else entirely?

It is huge topic spanning dozens of very different thinkers across a range of (implicitly converging) disciplines, from philosophy and political science to art and literature. The term has many specific usages and many usages that aren't specific. One simple way of putting it that clears up some common misconceptions is that philosophically postmodernism is basically a trend arising as a critique of the era of post-modernity, through the suspicion of philosophical modernism.

The era of post-modernity came about as a natural progression of the unstable dynamics latent in modernity (which can be traced to the Enlightenment or perhaps even earlier to the Reformation). While postmodernism was a natural philosophical progression of modernism which sought to descriptively come to terms with post-modernity and entailed suspicion of modernism once its instability/insufficiency became increasingly apparent.

It is hard for us to grasp the real scope of all this without having some background in the direction the grand project of modernism had been going since at least the Enlightenment and how it was pursuing the "end of history" (or some developmental finality) through discovering the grand underlying structure that organized everything in the world (Newton believed this to be math, to Hegel the spirit of freedom, etc.)

Various thinkers took to postmodernism in their own projects in very different ways, some indeed coming to the kind of general conclusions you mention, that of "truth" lacking an objective basis and so forth. However, that wasn't remotely universal among postmodern thinkers, some thought there was truth really "out there" and rejected the idea of infinite equally valid interpretations. In fact, even Lyotard's famous statement that 'postmodernism is a suspicion about metanarratives' was rejected by other postmodern thinkers, who defended certain formulations of grand overarching narratives.

Beyond that we have to discuss specific thinkers and manifestations of postmodernism else we will confuse those specific manifestations for the broad trend. Perhaps best to sum up by saying in short the mistake people make with postmodernism is in assuming a prescriptive rather than descriptive tone. That is, postmodernism attempts to express what is rather than what should be. It's about awareness and analysis, and awareness of your analysis, and awareness of your awareness of your analysis.

The problem with individuals like Stephen Hicks, Steven Pinker, Sokal and Bricmont, and of course Jordan Peterson, is through some failure, whether it be motivated bias and opportunism, intentional deception, or wading into a topic they don't give the proper time for and so settle with second-rate secondary sources for their understanding, they misconstrue postmodernism in the most facile and juvenile ways.

In Peterson's case it legitimately seems he hasn't taken the time to read primary sources and has erected this giant hodgepodge bogy-strawman mixing Marxists, post-structuralists, metaphysicians, and caricatured pomo themes which he equates as not only the foundation for the modern left but the very cause of all or most of the West's ills. He seems entirely unaware that Orthodox Marxists decried and warned about the ills of postmodernity and had sought to avoid it through their class-struggle, that Frankfurt school thinkers not only had nothing to do with post-structuralists but in some cases openly despised them, and that many postmodernists and post-structuralists were hostile to Marxists.

While it is true that much of the postmodern ethos did lend itself to circumstances and attitudes for a sort of cultural degeneration, his petty critiques of low hanging fruit completely ignore that the idealogical framework for all of this was laid down far before postmodernism, and that postmodernism didn't cause it but rather was a natural consequence of it. In fact, postmodernism isn't necessarily left-wing, with various early thinkers being explicit NatSocs, and in my view right-wing postmodernism is wholly required to not only shake off the decaying-yet-comfortable tatters of modernity but to subvert the hellscape that is postmodernity.
